q: Ames, a calendar-year individual, filed her 2024 income tax return on March 1, 2025. The return was due April 15, 2025, and contained no substantial omission of income or fraud. When does the general statute of limitations for assessing additional tax expire?
choices: April 15, 2028
March 1, 2028
April 15, 2031
March 1, 2031
exp: The IRS generally has three years from the later of the filing date or the due date to assess, and an early-filed return is treated as filed on the due date, so the period ends April 15, 2028. Counting from the actual March 1 filing date is the common error.

q: Burr, a calendar-year individual, filed his 2024 return on June 10, 2025, without an extension. No fraud or substantial omission is involved. When does the period for assessment expire?
choices: April 15, 2028
October 15, 2028
exp: For a late-filed return, the three-year assessment period runs from the date the return is actually filed, so it ends June 10, 2028. The due date is used only when the return is filed early.

q: Cruz reported gross income of $200,000 on her return but inadvertently omitted $60,000 of gross income that she should have reported. There was no fraud. What assessment period applies?
choices: Three years, because the omission was not fraudulent
Unlimited, because income was omitted
Six years, because the omission exceeds 25% of the gross income stated on the return
Seven years, because the omission exceeds 25% of the gross income stated on the return
exp: The assessment period is six years when the taxpayer omits gross income exceeding 25% of the gross income stated on the return: $60,000 ÷ $200,000 = 30%. An unlimited period applies only to fraud, a willful attempt to evade, or failure to file.

q: In which situation may the IRS assess tax at any time, with no statute of limitations?
choices: The taxpayer claimed a deduction that lacked substantial authority
The taxpayer omitted 30% of gross income through negligence
The taxpayer filed an amended return showing additional tax
The taxpayer filed a false or fraudulent return with intent to evade tax
exp: There is no limitation period for a false or fraudulent return with intent to evade tax, a willful attempt to evade tax, or a failure to file a return. A negligent omission over 25% of gross income extends the period to six years, not indefinitely.

q: Dion filed his 2022 return on April 15, 2023, and paid the tax shown. After an audit he paid an additional $8,000 on September 1, 2025. He now believes part of the $8,000 was not owed. What is the latest date he may file a refund claim for any portion of the $8,000?
choices: September 1, 2027
April 15, 2026
September 1, 2028
April 15, 2027
exp: A refund claim must be filed within the later of three years from the filing of the return (April 15, 2026) or two years from payment of the tax (September 1, 2027). A claim relying on the two-year rule is limited to tax paid within the two years, which covers the $8,000.

q: What is the period for filing a claim for refund attributable to a bad debt or a worthless security?
choices: Three years from the date the return was filed
Seven years from the due date of the return for the year the debt or security became worthless
Six years from the date the return was filed
Two years from the date the loss is discovered
exp: Because worthlessness is often hard to pin down, the refund period for bad debts and worthless securities is seven years from the due date of the return for the year of worthlessness. The six-year period concerns assessments for substantial omissions of income.

q: Ella filed her return three months late without an extension and paid the $10,000 balance due with the return. There was no reasonable cause or fraud. What are her total failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties?
exp: Failure-to-pay is 0.5% × 3 months × $10,000 = $150, and failure-to-file is 5% × 3 = 15% ($1,500) reduced by the $150 failure-to-pay penalty for the same months = $1,350, for a total of $1,500. Adding $1,500 and $150 without the offset gives $1,650.

q: Finn's correct tax liability was $80,000, but he reported only $60,000 on his individual return. No reasonable cause, adequate disclosure or substantial authority applies, and the understatement was not due to fraud. What accuracy-related penalty applies?
exp: An individual's understatement is substantial if it exceeds the greater of 10% of the correct tax ($8,000) or $5,000; the $20,000 understatement qualifies, and the penalty is 20% × $20,000 = $4,000. The 75% rate ($15,000) applies only to civil fraud.

q: The IRS proves by clear and convincing evidence that a portion of Gil's underpayment is attributable to fraud. What civil penalty applies to that portion?
choices: 75% of the underpayment attributable to fraud
20% of the underpayment attributable to fraud
40% of the underpayment attributable to fraud
100% of the underpayment attributable to fraud
exp: The civil fraud penalty equals 75% of the portion of the underpayment attributable to fraud, and the IRS bears the burden of proving fraud by clear and convincing evidence. The 20% rate is the accuracy-related penalty and 40% applies to gross valuation misstatements.

q: Which action can reduce the amount of an individual's understatement subject to the substantial-understatement penalty for a position that is not a tax shelter item?
choices: Filing the return on time
Adequately disclosing the position on the return when it has a reasonable basis
Paying the tax shown on the return in full
Obtaining an extension of time to file
exp: An understatement is reduced for items supported by substantial authority, or for items adequately disclosed (for example, on Form 8275) that have a reasonable basis. Timely filing and payment avoid other penalties but do not affect the accuracy-related penalty.

q: A paid preparer took an undisclosed position on a client's return that lacked substantial authority, and the preparer knew or reasonably should have known of the position. The conduct was not willful or reckless. The preparer's fee for the return was $3,000. What is the §6694 penalty?
exp: The penalty for an understatement due to an unreasonable position is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived from the return: 50% × $3,000 = $1,500. The $5,000 minimum applies to willful or reckless conduct.

q: A preparer willfully attempted to understate a client's tax liability on a return for which the preparer received a $10,000 fee. What is the §6694 penalty for willful or reckless conduct?
exp: For willful or reckless conduct, the penalty is the greater of $5,000 or 75% of the income derived from the return: 75% × $10,000 = $7,500. Using only the $5,000 minimum ignores the percentage alternative.

q: To avoid the §6694 preparer penalty for an unreasonable position, what support is required for a position that is NOT disclosed and is not a tax shelter or reportable transaction?
choices: Substantial authority
A reasonable basis
A realistic possibility of success
More likely than not
exp: An undisclosed position must be supported by substantial authority; a disclosed position needs only a reasonable basis. For tax shelters and reportable transactions, the preparer must reasonably believe the position is more likely than not to be sustained.

q: Under §7216, which disclosure of a client's tax return information by a preparer requires the client's written consent?
choices: Disclosure to another employee of the firm who helps prepare the return
Disclosure to a mortgage lender to support the client's loan application
Disclosure in connection with a quality or peer review
Disclosure in response to a court order
exp: Disclosing return information for a purpose other than preparing the return, such as providing it to a lender, requires the taxpayer's prior written consent. Disclosures within the firm for preparation, for peer review, or under a court order or subpoena are permitted without consent.

q: Which of the following is a preparer failure subject to an assessable penalty under §6695?
choices: Taking a position without substantial authority
Willfully understating a client's tax liability
Failing to furnish the taxpayer a copy of the completed return
Promoting an abusive tax shelter
exp: Section 6695 imposes penalties for procedural failures such as failing to furnish a copy of the return to the taxpayer, failing to sign, failing to provide a PTIN, failing to retain copies or lists, and failing to meet due diligence requirements. Understatement positions are covered by §6694 and shelter promotion by §6700.

q: While preparing a current-year return, a CPA learns that the client omitted income on a prior-year return. Under Circular 230, what must the CPA do?
choices: Notify the IRS of the omission immediately
Withdraw from the engagement immediately
File an amended return for the client
Promptly advise the client of the noncompliance and its consequences
exp: Section 10.21 requires a practitioner who knows of a client's noncompliance, error or omission to promptly advise the client of it and of the consequences under the law. The practitioner is not required to notify the IRS and may not file an amended return without the client's authorization.

q: Under Circular 230, may a practitioner rely on the work product of another person?
choices: Yes, if the practitioner used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training and evaluating that person
Never; the practitioner must independently verify all work
Only if the other person is also a CPA or attorney
Only if the client consents in writing
exp: Section 10.22 deems a practitioner to have exercised due diligence when relying on another person's work if the practitioner used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training and evaluating that person. There is no requirement that the person be credentialed or that the client consent.

q: For which engagement may a CPA charge a contingent fee?
choices: Preparing a client's original income tax return, with the fee based on the refund obtained
Representing a client in a judicial proceeding arising under the Internal Revenue Code
Preparing an original return for a fee equal to a percentage of the tax savings
Advising on a tax plan, with the fee based on future tax savings
exp: Contingent fees are permitted for representing a client in a judicial proceeding, for services connected with an IRS examination of or challenge to an original return, and for claims solely for statutory interest or penalties. They are prohibited for preparing an original return under Circular 230 and the AICPA Code.

q: A client who disputes a CPA's fee requests the return of the original records the client provided for preparing the return. What must the CPA do under Circular 230?
choices: Return the records only after the fee is paid
Return copies but keep the originals until the dispute is resolved
Promptly return the client's records necessary to comply with federal tax obligations, although the CPA may keep copies
Send the records to the IRS to hold until the dispute is resolved
exp: Section 10.28 requires a practitioner, on request, to promptly return any records of the client necessary for the client to comply with federal tax obligations, even during a fee dispute; the practitioner may retain copies. Holding records hostage for payment is prohibited.

q: Which person may represent a taxpayer before all offices of the IRS, including the Independent Office of Appeals, on any tax matter?
choices: An unenrolled return preparer who prepared the return
A bookkeeper with a PTIN
An enrolled retirement plan agent
A CPA in good standing
exp: Attorneys, CPAs and enrolled agents have unlimited practice rights before the IRS. Unenrolled preparers have only limited rights for returns they prepared, and enrolled actuaries and retirement plan agents are limited to plan-related matters.

q: A CPA is asked to represent two clients whose interests in an IRS matter conflict. Under Circular 230, the CPA may proceed if the CPA reasonably believes she can provide competent and diligent representation to each, the representation is not prohibited by law, and:
choices: Each affected client gives informed consent, confirmed in writing
The CPA notifies the IRS of the conflict
The CPA obtains oral consent from one of the clients
The CPA charges each client a reduced fee
exp: Section 10.29 requires informed consent from each affected client confirmed in writing, generally within 30 days, and the practitioner must retain the written consents for at least 36 months after the representation ends. Notifying the IRS does not cure a conflict.

q: A client tells a CPA preparing his return that he had $12,000 of business travel expenses. Nothing in the client's other information suggests the amount is incorrect or incomplete. Under Circular 230, what is the CPA's obligation?
choices: The CPA must examine receipts for every expense before signing
The CPA may rely in good faith on the client's information without verification, but must make reasonable inquiries if information appears incorrect or incomplete
The CPA must refuse to deduct expenses the CPA did not personally observe
The CPA must attach a disclaimer to the return
exp: A practitioner may generally rely in good faith on information furnished by the client without verification but may not ignore implications of other information and must make reasonable inquiries when information appears incorrect, inconsistent or incomplete. Independent verification of all items is not required, though substantiation rules such as those for travel should be discussed.

q: Which sanction is NOT one the Treasury Department may impose on a practitioner under Circular 230?
choices: Censure
Disbarment from practice before the IRS
Imprisonment
A monetary penalty
exp: Circular 230 sanctions include censure (public reprimand), suspension, disbarment, and monetary penalties against the practitioner or the firm. Imprisonment results only from a criminal prosecution under the Internal Revenue Code, not from Circular 230 proceedings.

q: Which type of IRS examination is generally conducted at the taxpayer's place of business and is the most comprehensive?
choices: Correspondence examination
Office examination
Document matching review
Field examination
exp: Field examinations are conducted by revenue agents at the taxpayer's business or the representative's office and are used for complex business returns. Correspondence audits are handled by mail for simple issues, and office audits take place at an IRS office.

q: After an examination, the IRS issued a statutory notice of deficiency to a taxpayer residing in the United States. Within what period must the taxpayer petition the Tax Court to contest the deficiency without first paying it?
choices: 90 days from the mailing of the notice
30 days from the mailing of the notice
150 days from the mailing of the notice
Two years from the mailing of the notice
exp: A taxpayer has 90 days from the mailing of the statutory notice of deficiency (150 days if it is addressed to a person outside the United States) to petition the Tax Court. The 30-day period relates to the earlier letter offering an Appeals conference.

q: A taxpayer wants to litigate a proposed deficiency before a jury. Which forum must the taxpayer use?
choices: The U.S. Tax Court, after filing a petition
A U.S. District Court, after paying the tax and suing for a refund
The U.S. Court of Federal Claims, without paying the tax
The IRS Independent Office of Appeals
exp: A jury trial is available only in a U.S. District Court refund suit, which requires paying the tax first and filing a refund claim. The Tax Court requires no prepayment but has no jury, and the Court of Federal Claims also requires payment and has no jury.

q: Which statement about the IRS Independent Office of Appeals is correct?
choices: It may not settle cases; it can only sustain or reverse the examiner
A taxpayer may go to Appeals only after a Tax Court petition is filed
It may settle cases by weighing the hazards of litigation
Its decisions may not be challenged in court
exp: Appeals is independent of the examination function and may settle cases based on the hazards of litigation, which examiners generally may not do. Taxpayers typically reach Appeals by filing a protest in response to a 30-day letter, and unresolved cases can still go to court.

q: Which statement about interest on a federal income tax underpayment is correct?
choices: Interest is waived if the taxpayer shows reasonable cause for the underpayment
Interest is deductible by individuals as an itemized deduction
Interest runs only from the date the IRS issues a notice of deficiency
Interest runs from the original due date of the return until paid and generally cannot be avoided by showing reasonable cause
exp: Underpayment interest accrues from the return's original due date (without regard to extensions) until payment, at the federal short-term rate plus 3 percentage points, compounded daily. Reasonable cause can excuse many penalties but not interest, and individuals cannot deduct it.

q: During an examination of Hale's return, the assessment period is about to expire. How may the period be extended?
choices: By a written agreement between Hale and the IRS signed before the period expires
By the IRS issuing a 30-day letter
Automatically, whenever an examination is in progress
By the IRS filing a notice of federal tax lien
exp: The assessment period for income tax may be extended by a written agreement (such as Form 872) executed by the taxpayer and the IRS before the period expires. An open examination or a 30-day letter does not by itself stop the statute from running.

q: Which person is a tax return preparer subject to the §6694 understatement penalties?
choices: A friend who prepares a neighbor's return free of charge
A person who, for compensation, prepares a substantial portion of a return or claim for refund
An employee who prepares only the return of her own employer
A software company whose program a taxpayer uses to prepare his own return
exp: A tax return preparer is any person who prepares for compensation, or employs others to prepare for compensation, all or a substantial portion of a return or refund claim. Uncompensated preparers, employees preparing their employer's return, and providers of mechanical assistance such as software are excluded.
